title: Leaders Who Veto Decisions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece treats a leader's veto power as a last resort, not a routine tool, because overriding a group's carefully reached decision signals distrust in the team's judgment and can erode future participation. The author acknowledges legitimate reasons leaders might want to intervene, quality control, unintended consequences, overlooked information, but insists a veto should only be used when the consequences of letting the decision stand would be genuinely severe. Notably, the piece recommends that leaders explain their reasoning and ask the team to voluntarily withdraw the decision first, using the veto only if persuasion fails. It closes with a pointed challenge to reflect on how often a leader has actually used this power.
points: A veto tells a team the leader believes their own judgment outranks the group's, at real cost to trust
Good leaders reserve vetoes for decisions that would irreparably harm the organization
Best practice: explain the reasoning and ask the team to voluntarily withdraw the decision before vetoing
Frequent vetoes destroy a team's motivation to invest effort in reaching quality decisions
quotes: Good leaders reserve their veto power for situations and decisions that would irreparably harm the organization or undermine a major initiative.
A veto says loudly that the leader believes they are smarter, wiser, and more clairvoyant than the team entrusted with the decision.

Unless the group becomes convinced of the leader’s wisdom for standing in the way, a veto will erode trust, diminish future participation, and leave the impression that the team’s input is undervalued.
The best leaders even go one step further. They ask the team to withdraw their decision based on their argument.
A leader who asserts their decision rights for any other reason is taking a big gamble.
